procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of acquittal passed on April 4, 1968, in cases where the appellant alleged that officers of the respondent had committed an offense under the Companies Act, 1956.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (complainant) presented petitions of appeal to the Calcutta High Court on July 1, 1968, challenging the orders of acquittal. The High Court did not entertain the appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the Calcutta High Court did not entertain the appeals. The Supreme Court was reviewing the judgment and order dated August 13, 1968, of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Appeals Nos. 425 to 428 of 1968.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appeal against an order of acquittal in a case instituted upon a complaint is competent without an application for and grant of special leave under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The case involved appeals against orders of acquittal.
The original cases were instituted upon a complaint, not by the state.
The complainants filed appeals directly to the High Court.
Crucially, the complainants did not file any application to the High Court for "special leave to appeal" as required by the Code of Criminal Procedure.
law: Section 404 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) establishes that an appeal is a statutory right and can only be filed as provided for by the Code or another law.
Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C. specifically governs appeals against acquittal in cases instituted upon a complaint.

This section requires a two-step process: first, the complainant must make an application to the High Court for "special leave to appeal," and second, only if the High Court grants this special leave can the complainant present the actual appeal.
Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. sets a time limit of 60 days from the date of acquittal to apply for this special leave.
Article 114 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requires that once special leave is granted, the appeal must be filed within 30 days.
application: The Supreme Court applied the clear mandate of Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C. to the facts of the case.
The Court noted that the right to appeal is not automatic and must follow the prescribed procedure.
In this case, the complainants failed to follow the mandatory first step of the procedure: they never applied for special leave to appeal.
Because no application for special leave was made, no special leave was granted.
The Court reasoned that without the grant of special leave, any appeal filed under this section is legally incompetent and cannot be entertained by the High Court.
Furthermore, the Court noted that the appeals were also barred by limitation, as the 60-day window to even apply for leave had expired.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an appeal against an order of acquittal in a case instituted upon a complaint is not competent unless the complainant first applies for and is granted special leave to appeal by the High Court, as required by Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Since this mandatory pre-condition was not met, the appeals were rejected as incompetent and barred by limitation.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appeal against an acquittal is maintainable if it is filed beyond the period of limitation prescribed under Section 417(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 114 of the Limitation Act, 1963.

facts: Appeals were filed in the High Court against an order of acquittal in a case instituted upon a complaint.
The High Court rejected the appeals, holding they were barred by the limitation period prescribed in Article 114 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The appellant contended that the appeals were filed under the Companies Act and not Section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), and therefore the limitation periods did not apply.
law: Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C. governs appeals against acquittals in cases instituted upon a complaint.
This section requires a two-step process: first, the complainant must apply to the High Court for 'special leave to appeal'.
Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. mandates that this application for special leave must be filed within 60 days from the date of the acquittal order.
Article 114 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requires that once special leave is granted, the actual appeal must be filed within 30 days from the date of the grant.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the right to appeal in this case was governed by Section 417 of the Cr.P.C., not the Companies Act.
The Court found that the appeals were rightly rejected by the High Court for three main reasons:
1. No application for the grant of special leave was ever made to the High Court, as required by Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C.
2. Without the grant of special leave, the appeals were legally incompetent and could not be entertained.

3. Because the mandatory pre-condition of applying for and obtaining special leave was not met, the appeals were consequently barred by limitation under both Section 417(4) of the Cr.P.C. and Article 114 of the Limitation Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that an appeal against an acquittal from a case instituted upon a complaint is not maintainable if the mandatory procedure is not followed. The complainant must first apply for special leave to appeal within 60 days of the acquittal (S. 417(4) Cr.P.C.), and only after leave is granted, file the appeal within 30 days (Art. 114 Limitation Act). Since no application for special leave was ever filed, the appeals were incompetent and barred by limitation.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 624B of the Companies Act confers an independent right of appeal from an order of acquittal passed by a criminal court.

law.description: An appeal is a creature of statute. This section states that no appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a Criminal Court except as provided for by the Code of Criminal Procedure or by any other law.
This section governs the right to appeal in cases of acquittal. It allows the State Government to direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the High Court.

application.description: The Court first established that the right to appeal is not inherent and must be explicitly conferred by a statute, as laid out in Section 404 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).

The Court then analyzed the text of Section 624B of the Companies Act. It found that the section's language only speaks of the Central Government directing or authorizing a person to *present* an appeal. It does not contain language that creates or confers a substantive right to appeal itself.
The Court determined that the actual right to appeal from an acquittal in this case is governed by Section 417 of the Cr.P.C.

It compared Section 624B of the Companies Act to Section 417(1) of the Cr.P.C., concluding they are similar provisions. Both sections are procedural, empowering a government entity (Central or State) to have an appeal presented by a designated person, rather than creating the right of appeal itself.

To illustrate what a right-conferring section looks like, the Court contrasted Section 624B with Section 483 of the Companies Act. Section 483 explicitly states that appeals *shall lie* from certain orders, thereby creating a clear right of appeal, which Section 624B fails to do.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that Section 624B of the Companies Act does not confer an independent right of appeal. The Court reasoned that this section is merely a procedural provision that specifies who the Central Government may authorize to present an appeal. The substantive right to appeal from an order of acquittal is governed by Section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appeal against an order of acquittal in a case instituted upon a complaint is competent without an application for and grant of special leave under Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that an application for special leave was not required because their right to appeal was independently conferred by Section 624B of the Companies Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appeal against an acquittal is maintainable if it is filed beyond the period of limitation prescribed under Section 417(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 114 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
appellant_arguments: The appellant filed the appeals after the prescribed limitation period, implicitly arguing that the appeal was maintainable, likely on the grounds that Section 624B of the Companies Act provided a special right of appeal not governed by the general limitation periods.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 624B of the Companies Act confers an independent right of appeal from an order of acquittal passed by a criminal court.
appellant_arguments: The right of appeal is conferred by section 624B of the Companies Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 624B of the Companies Act does not confer a substantive right of appeal from an order of acquittal. This section only authorizes a specific person to present an appeal, the right to which is governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: A provision in the Companies Act which does confer a right of appeal is section 483, which applies to orders and decisions in the matter of winding up a company.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 624B of the Companies Act does not confer an independent right of appeal from an order of acquittal. It only empowers the Central Government to direct or authorize a person to present an appeal. Any such appeal must still comply with the procedural requirements of the Code of Criminal Procedure, specifically the requirement to apply for and be granted special leave under Section 417(3) and to file the appeal within the prescribed period of limitation.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation of Section 404 Cr.P.C., which provides that no appeal shall lie from a criminal court order except as provided by the Code or any other law.
Analysis of Section 417(3) Cr.P.C., which requires a complainant to obtain special leave from the High Court to appeal an order of acquittal.

Application of the limitation periods prescribed in Section 417(4) Cr.P.C. (60 days for an application for special leave) and Article 114 of the Limitation Act, 1963 (30 days to file the appeal after leave is granted).
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's primary argument that Section 624B of the Companies Act confers a right of appeal was rejected. The court found that "s. 6248 does not confer any right of appeal from an order of acquittal passed by a criminal court... It only empowers the Central Government to present appeals through persons mentioned therein."
The appellant failed to file an application for the grant of special leave to appeal as required by Section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Because no special leave was granted, the appeals were deemed incompetent. The court stated, "An appeal under section 417 ( 3) against acquittal is competent only when there is special leave granted by the High Court."

The appeals were barred by limitation. No application for special leave was made within the 60-day period under Section 417(4) Cr.P.C., and consequently, the appeal was not filed within 30 days of any grant of leave as required by Article 114 of the Limitation Act.
why_respondent_won: The respondent won because the appellant's appeals were procedurally invalid and legally unsustainable. The court upheld the strict procedural framework for appeals against acquittal established by the Code of Criminal Procedure, which the appellant failed to follow. The appeals were correctly rejected by the High Court for being filed without special leave and for being time-barred.
